grh_20f6ec8aca7b6acbc61e.title: Prelude To Thanksgiving
paragraphs: Teenager Katherine Anne 'Tanny' Gardner loves her mother but thinks the adults around her are hopelessly old-fashioned. A self-described tomboy, she is especially close to football star Randy Billings and resents glamorous newcomer Jean West. Randy first sides with Tanny's mother against Tanny riding on Bud Collins's motorcycle, then awkwardly tells Tanny that Jean has maneuvered him into taking her to the Thanksgiving football dance. Hurt and jealous, Tanny defiantly accepts Bud's offer of a motorcycle ride even as Randy tries to forbid it. Just after they start off, a truck skids around the corner and Tanny is badly hurt. She escapes internal injury but suffers heavy bruising and a broken arm. The accident forces Randy to admit that he had taken Tanny for granted and that jealousy and his own careless words pushed her toward Bud. As Tanny recovers, Randy chooses Thanksgiving dinner at her bedside over the dance, gives her his fraternity pin and makes clear that she is the girl he wants. Tanny, suddenly less certain that her mother's advice is obsolete, asks her mother what being in love feels like.

This [[show|dr-christian|Dr. Christian]] broadcast aired on November 22, 1939. It is listed as episode 55 in the archive. [[org|org.8480b75bc0c36e4b|CBS Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Jean Hersholt and Rosemary De Camp. Other credited names include Art Gilmore as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 29 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.b199d95f77b6c241|Vaseline]].

grh_20c29fdccd1a299cc864.title: The Cross and the Arrow
paragraphs: German tank-factory worker Willie Wegler becomes disgusted by forced labor, militarism and his own part in feeding the Nazi war machine. He arranges hay in the shape of an arrow and sets it alight to guide British bombers toward the hidden factory, but is shot and drawn into a Gestapo investigation. The authorities conceal the truth and blame a Polish forced laborer to protect factory morale. Wegler survives long enough to see the bombers return, satisfied that his signal was seen and hoping his act of refusal will inspire others.

The surviving recording runs about 30 minutes.
